name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679, General Data Protection Regulation
status_note: Applies from 25 May 2018 in the 27 EU member states (Art. 99(2)). Incorporated into the EEA Agreement for Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway by EEA Joint Committee Decision No 154/2018 of 6 July 2018. The exact EEA entry-into-force date was not confirmed from a primary source today.

rights.summary: The data subject can obtain erasure without undue delay where a listed ground applies, for example the data are no longer necessary, consent is withdrawn, the person objects under Art. 21, or the processing is unlawful.

The data subject can object to processing based on legitimate interests or public interest, and the controller must stop unless it shows compelling legitimate grounds, and can object to direct marketing at any time without conditions.

rights.citation: Art. 17 and Art. 21, CJEU C-131/12 Google Spain (13 May 2014)
rights.summary: A search engine operator is a controller and can be required to remove links from results for a search on a person's name, even when the publication on the source page is lawful, unless the public interest in access prevails, for example because of the person's role in public life.
The data subject can obtain confirmation of whether their data are processed, a copy, and information on the source.
The data subject can have inaccurate personal data corrected without undue delay.

deadline.extension_note: The controller must act without undue delay and within one month of receipt. It may extend by two further months where necessary given complexity and number of requests, but must tell the data subject within the first month and give reasons. If it will not act, it must say so within one month and mention the right to complain and seek a judicial remedy (Art. 12(4)).

identity_verification: Where the controller has reasonable doubts about the requester's identity, it may ask for additional information necessary to confirm it (Art. 12(6)). The EDPB says verification must be proportionate and that asking for a copy of an ID card is often excessive (EDPB Guidelines 01/2022, section 3.3).

authorized_agent.citation: EDPB Guidelines 01/2022 on the right of access, paras 80 and 81, GDPR Art. 80
authorized_agent.note: The GDPR does not regulate representation directly. The EDPB says a third party, such as a proxy or a legal guardian of a minor, may make a request on behalf of the data subject, that national rules on powers of attorney apply, and that the controller may verify the authorisation. A data subject may also mandate a qualifying not-for-profit body to lodge a complaint for them (Art. 80(1)).

special_channels.name: Google personal information removal request under European privacy law
special_channels.note: Google's Right to be Forgotten overview links to this form and says it delists URLs from results for countries that apply European data protection law. Delisting is not applied outside the EU.

special_channels.name: Bing request form to block search results in Europe
special_channels.note: For European residents. The country list includes EU and EEA states, Switzerland and the United Kingdom. Asks for legal name, search names, country, exact URLs, role in public life, and a signed statement. Supporting documents can be attached.

public_records_note: The GDPR has no general exemption for publicly available personal data. A people-search site that compiles public data is still a controller and must have a legal basis, usually legitimate interests under Art. 6(1)(f), which an Art. 21 objection directly challenges. Erasure can be refused where processing is necessary for freedom of expression and information, a legal obligation, public interest archiving, or legal claims (Art. 17(3)), and member states set their own journalistic and expression exemptions under Art. 85. The Google Spain ruling allows delisting from name searches even when the source page stays lawful.
